# Introduction

Prostate cancer (PCa) is the second most commonly diagnosed cancer among men worldwide and a leading cause of cancer-related mortality [@bray2024]. Although early detection can reduce deaths from PCa, population screening with prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is limited by false positives, overdiagnosis, and overtreatment, particularly of indolent disease [@ilic2013; @roobol2025]. Therefore, there is a clinical need to identify men at elevated risk of clinically significant or metastatic PCa to focus early screening and downstream diagnostics (e.g., MRI), while minimizing harms.

PCa is highly heritable [~42%: @lichtenstein2000] with risk influenced by rare pathogenic variants (RPVs) as well as common variants. RPVs, such as BRCA1, BRCA2, and HOXB13, confer large increases in risk but occur at low frequencies in the general population [@seibert2023]. Polygenic models combine many variants with small effects to estimate inherited risk. Furthermore, polygenic hazard scores (PHS) use time-to-event modeling to predict age at diagnosis, enabling prioritization of early-onset disease which is at greater risk of clinical significance [@desikan2017; @seibert2018; @huynh-le2021]. These models are beginning to be implemented in a clinical trial of precision prostate cancer screening in the United States Department of Veterans Affairs healthcare system (Clinicaltrials.gov NCT05926102).

Recent PCa PHS models were developed in large, multi-ethnic cohorts and show robust stratification, but external validation in Nordic populations is limited. Here, we perform external validation of the latest age-of-onset model, PHS601 [@vassy2024], in two Norwegian cohorts: a population study (Hordaland Health Studies; HUSK) and a clinical cohort enriched for family history of cancer (Norwegian Familial Cancer Study; NFCS) [@mattingsdal2021]. We evaluate whether PHS601 stratifies risk of PCa and aggressive PCa. We also leverage whole-genome sequencing to compare PHS-based risk stratification with RPV carrier status, including HOXB13. Our aim is to establish the performance of PHS601 for age-specific risk prediction in Norwegian men as a step toward local implementation in a prospective clinical trial of genomically-informed cancer screening. 

# Methods

## Study Population

Two Norwegian cohorts were included in this study. The first cohort was the Hordaland Health Studies (Helseundersøkelsene i Hordaland; HUSK). This cohort was recruited from Rogaland county in western Norway in two waves. The first wave was in 1992/1993 and the second wave was in 1997/1999. HUSK participants were genotyped at deCODE Genetics (https://www.decode.com/) in two batches (10,083 and 25,432 individuals in batch 1 and 2, respectively) using a customized Illumina GSA v3 array (687,316 genotyped variants). Prior to phasing and imputation, genotyping data were QCed separately for each batch using plink2 [@purcell2007]. QC steps for variants included removal of indels, non-ATGC, strand-ambiguous, poorly-genotyped (plink2's option: --geno 0.05), non-autosomal and rare (--maf 0.05) variants as well as variants with extreme deviation from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (--hwe 1E-50 midp keep-fewhet). Chromosomal strand and allele order for the remaining variants were aligned based on the HGDP + 1KG reference panel from gnomAD [@koenig2024], and variants with alleles that were not possible to align to the reference as well as variants with MAF deviating from the reference by more than 30% were removed. Resulting genotypes from two batches were merged. Variants with high missingness (--geno 0.02) and individuals with poor genotyping rate (--mind 0.05) were removed from the merged data. The combined dataset was then phased and imputed with Beagle 5.4 (version 27May24.118) using the HGDP + 1KG reference panel. The resulting dataset contained 10,531,075 autosomal variants and 35,476 individuals.

The second cohort was the Norwegian Familial Cancer Study (NFCS) [@mattingsdal2021]. Participants in this cohort were recruited in 1980-1995 from all of Norway via self-report based on over-representation of cancer in their families. Genomic DNA was extracted from peripheral blood samples using the DNeasy Blood & Tissue Kit (Qiagen, Germantown, MD, USA), following the manufacturer’s protocol, and analyzed using the Illumina OmniExpress 24 v1.1 chip at deCODE genetics (Reykjavik, Iceland). The genotyped dataset consisted of 15,769 participants with 713,014 SNPs. Genotype data were imputed using the HRC v1.1 reference panel following the same imputation protocol as The Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort [@corfield2024]. After imputation, the dataset consisted of 7,526,252 autosomal SNPs. 

## Characterization of PCa Cases

PCa cases were defined as participants with ICD10 code C61. Diagnosis date was the first instance of this ICD10 code in the Cancer Registry of Norway, which has been found to be 98.8% complete [@larsen2009]. Controls were limited to males (excluding those censored before age 40, since no diagnoses were observed before that age) and censored at age of last observation. We did not remove individuals with other cancer diagnoses. Aggressive disease was defined according to metastasis codes `{r} metastase_strict[1:length(metastase_strict)-1]`, and `{r} metastase_strict[length(metastase_strict)]` in the Norwegian Cancer Registry, corresponding to disease that extends to lymph nodes inside or outside the same body region, organ metastasis outside the body region, and microscopic or macroscopic ingrowth into neighboring structures. 

## Harmonize alleles and calculate PHSes

 The list of variants used by the PHS601 model, and their effect sizes, were acquired by contacting the authors [@vassy2024]. Chromosome X imputation was not available in our genotype data so the 21 SNPs in the original model on chromosome X were removed leaving 580 SNPs. Imputed genotype data in each cohort and model variants were matched by genomic position and alleles, resulting in 519 variants (in HUSK) and 557 variants (in NFCS) used for PHS computation. Strand-ambiguous variants were retained, after verifying that no strand flips were present among non-strand ambiguous SNPs in either of the two cohorts. Polygenic hazard scores were calculated for each cohort using `plink -score`.

## Sequencing and variant calling

Variant calling was performed using the CPSR package [@nakken2021]. We identified individuals with genetic variants from ClinVar that were classified as "pathogenic" in at least one copy of RPVs known to be associated with increased risk of PCa, including mutations within the genes BRCA1, BRCA2, ATM, PALB2, CHEK2, HOXB13, MLH1, MSH2, MSH6, PMS2, TP53, and EPCAM. The HOXB13 G84E SNP was included in PHS601 and all individuals with this SNP imputed also have the mutation in the WGS data.

## Statistics

Polygenic hazard scores were evaluated in both cohorts using Cox proportional hazards models using the `coxph` function from the `survival` package in `R` [@survival-package]. For the any-stage-PCa model, events were defined as age of first PCa diagnosis, and controls were censored at age of last observation. For the aggressive-PCa model, events were defined as age of first aggressive disease diagnosis. Polygenic hazard scores were centered and scaled prior to model fit. Performance of each model is reported as HR, which represents the increase in risk for a one-SD increase in PHS, with 95% confidence intervals (CI) and p-values. In addition, we used the metrics of HR~80/20~, which is the hazard ratio between the top 20% and the bottom 20% of PHS, HR~80/50~, which is the hazard ratio between the top 20% and the median PHS, as well as Harrell's concordance index (C-index). For these three metrics, 95% confidence intervals were generated using `{r} bootstrap_iters` bootstrap iterations. For plotting of incidence curves, participants were separated by centile range of PHS into the top 20%, the bottom 20%, and the middle 60%. All Cox models were evaluated for the proportional hazards assumption using `cox.zph` and by inspecting plots of the Schoenfeld residuals versus time [@grambsch1994]. For models that did not meet these assumptions, we performed sensitivity analysis with time-dependent covariates and a linear time transform (i.e., PHS $\cdot$ age) for the time-dependent PHS with the `tt` function. 

Next, we assessed the effect of RPVs on risk prediction, using WGS data from the NFCS cohort. To test whether RPVs were at higher frequency in cases than in controls, we used the one-sided Fisher's exact. We tested this for each of the twelve RPVs and for a separate variable indicating if participants carried any of the RPVs for a total of 13 tests. The p-values from the Fisher's tests were adjusted using the Benjamini & Hochberg correction. The one gene at elevated frequency in the cases (HOXB13) was then used in a Cox survival analysis to estimate the risk of PCa associated with carrying this pathogenic variant. This model was evaluated based on the HR between carriers and non-carriers as well as the C-index. To test whether individuals with high PHS were more likely to carry a rare variant, we used logistic regression. To compare the HOXB13 carriers to PHS, we subgrouped the dataset for individuals with both WGS and genotyping, refit the Cox model of PHS with this smaller sample, and calculated the HR for a similar proportion of individuals as were HOXB13 carriers. In this case, 1.7% of participants carried a HOXB13 mutation so we calculated the HR between the top 1.7% of PHS and the median subject. 

To evaluate how generalizable our results were to the population of Norway, we compared the cumulative incidence in each cohort for both PCa (any stage) and for aggressive PCa to the cumulative incidence from the Cancer Registry of Norway (using the same ICD10 code and metastasis codes as before). We used cancer registry data for PCa cases in Norway for the years 2014-2017 as reported by @huynh-le2020a as annualized age-specific incidence rate binned by 5-year age groups. To convert 5-year incidence rate into cumulative incidence, we fit an exponential model to the average incidence for each 5-year age group. For PCa, the best fit was an exponential quadratic and for aggressive PCa the best fit was an exponential. We then predicted the annualized incidence from this model and calculated the cumulative incidence rate from the cumulative sum of cases. We compared these to the cumulative incidence rates derived from the Cox PH model for each phenotype (PCa or aggressive PCa) in each cohort (@{suppfig-comp}). We then stratified the cumulative incidence curves by the HRs corresponding to the top 20% and bottom 20% of PHS from the Cox proportional hazards model fit to the HUSK data, as described below.

# Results

## PHS601 strongly stratified PCa risk in two Norwegian cohorts

PHS601 strongly stratified PCa risk in both Norwegian cohorts. In the HUSK cohort (`{r} p2521_sample_size[1, 3]` cases and  `{r} format(p2521_sample_size[[1, 4]], big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)` controls), each SD increase in PHS was associated with an `r (round(p2521_coxph_results[1, "estimate"], 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk of PCa (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_coxph_results[1, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_coxph_results[1, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_coxph_results[1, "conf.high"], 2))`], p `{r} pvalr(p2521_coxph_results[[1, "p.value"]])`; @{tbl-1}). Individuals in the top quintile of PHS had over `{r} floor(p2521[2, 3])` times the risk of those in the bottom quintile (HR~80/20~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521[2, 3], 2))`, 95\% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521[2, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521[2, 5], 2))`\]) and `{r} (round(p2521[4, 3], 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk than the median individual (HR~80/50~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521[4, 3], 2))`, 95\% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521[4, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521[4, 5], 2))`\]; @{fig-phs}A). Results were similar in the NFCS cohort (`{r} p212_sample_size[1, 3]` cases and `{r} p212_sample_size[1, 4]` controls), where each SD increase in PHS conferred a twofold greater risk (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_coxph_results[1, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_coxph_results[1, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_coxph_results[1, "conf.high"], 2))`], p `{r} pvalr(p212_coxph_results[[1, "p.value"]])`; @{tbl-1}), with HR~80/20~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212[2, 3], 2))` (95\% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212[2, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212[2, 5], 2))`\]) and HR~80/50~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212[4, 3], 2))` (95\% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212[4, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212[4, 5], 2))`\]; @{fig-phs}B).

In both cohorts, proportional hazards tests and plots of weighted residuals revealed a negative trend in hazard ratios with age (HUSK: $\chi^2$ = `r round(p2521_zph[1, "chisq"], 2)`, p = `r pvalr(p2521_zph[1, "p"])`; NFCS: $\chi^2$ = `r round(p212_zph[1, "chisq"], 2)`, p = `r pvalr(p212_zph[1, "p"])`; @{suppfig-zph}) indicating that the effect of PHS diminished with age. To model this, we fit an extended Cox model with a linear time-dependent PHS term (intercept at age 40). At age 40, each SD increase in PHS was associated with a `{r} sprintf("%.1f", round(p2521_coxph_results[3, "estimate"], 1))`-fold (HUSK: HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_coxph_results[3, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_coxph_results[3, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_coxph_results[3, "conf.high"], 2))`], p `{r} pvalr(p2521_coxph_results[[3, "p.value"]])`) and `{r} sprintf("%.1f", round(p212_coxph_results[3, "estimate"], 0))`-fold (NFCS: HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_coxph_results[3, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_coxph_results[3, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_coxph_results[3, "conf.high"], 2))`], p `{r} pvalr(p212_coxph_results[[3, "p.value"]])`) higher risk, declining by approximately `r round(1 - p2521_coxph_results[4, "estimate"], 3) * 100`\% and `r round(1 - p212_coxph_results[4, "estimate"], 3) * 100`\% per year, respectively (HUSK: HR = `{r} sprintf("%.3f", round(p2521_coxph_results[4, "estimate"], 3))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.3f", round(p2521_coxph_results[4, "conf.low"], 3))`, `{r} sprintf("%.3f", round(p2521_coxph_results[4, "conf.high"], 3))`], p `{r} pvalr(p2521_coxph_results[[4, "p.value"]])`; NFCS: HR = `{r} sprintf("%.3f", round(p212_coxph_results[4, "estimate"], 3))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.3f", round(p212_coxph_results[4, "conf.low"], 3))`, `{r} sprintf("%.3f", round(p212_coxph_results[4, "conf.high"], 3))`], p `{r} pvalr(p212_coxph_results[[4, "p.value"]])`). However, the time-varying effects were weak and residual plots showed high variability, so we present the simpler proportional hazards models in the main results and figures.

Together, these results confirm that PHS601 effectively stratifies PCa risk in both Norwegian cohorts, with modest evidence for age-dependent attenuation of its effect. 

## PHS601 was associated with aggressive PCa in Norwegian cohorts

In addition to evaluating the performance of PHS601 in stratifying individuals based on risk of PCa at any stage, we were also interested in the association of PHS601 with aggressive disease. In the HUSK cohort (`{r} p2521_sample_size[2, 3]` aggressive cases and `{r} format(p2521_sample_size[[2, 4]], big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)` controls), each SD increase in PHS was associated with a `{r} (round(p2521_coxph_results[2, "estimate"], 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk of aggressive disease (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_coxph_results[2, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_coxph_results[2, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_coxph_results[2, "conf.high"], 2))`], p `{r} pvalr(p2521_coxph_results[[2, "p.value"]])`; @{tbl-1}). Individuals in the top quintile of PHS had `{r} floor(p2521_meta[2, 3])`-fold greater risk of aggressive disease than individuals in the bottom quintile (HR~80/20~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_meta[2, 3], 2))`, 95% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_meta[2, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_meta[2, 5], 2))`\]) and `{r} (round(p2521_meta[4, 3], 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk than the median individual (HR~80/50~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_meta[4, 3], 2))`, 95% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_meta[4, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p2521_meta[4, 5], 2))`\]; @{fig-meta}A). Similarily, in the NFCS cohort (`{r} p212_sample_size[2, 3]` aggressive cases and `{r} format(p212_sample_size[[2, 4]], big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)` controls), each SD increase in PHS conferred a `{r} (round(p212_coxph_results[2, "estimate"], 2) * 100) - 100`\% greater risk of aggressive disease (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_coxph_results[2, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_coxph_results[2, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_coxph_results[2, "conf.high"], 2))`], p `{r} pvalr(p212_coxph_results[[2, "p.value"]])`; @{tbl-1}), with HR~80/20~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_meta[2, 3], 2))` (95% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_meta[2, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_meta[2, 5], 2))`\]) and HR~80/50~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_meta[4, 3], 2))` (95% CI \[`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_meta[4, 4], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(p212_meta[4, 5], 2))`\]; @{fig-meta}B). Proportional hazards assumptions were not violated in either cohort based on statistical tests and weighted residual plots (statistics, Figure S1).

## HOXB13 effect on PCa risk was not independent of PHS in the NFCS cohort

We compared RPVs and PHS in predicting PCa risk in the NFCS cohort (as the HUSK cohort does not include WGS data). Analyses were restricted to `{r} wgs_summary$wgs_1` participants with both WGS and genotyping (`{r} wgs_summary$status_1` cases and `{r} wgs_summary$wgs_1 - wgs_summary$status_1` controls) of whom `{r} wgs_summary$any_carrier_1` carried a predisposing mutation in one of the target genes. As only HOXB13 mutations were enriched among cases (OR = `r sprintf("%.2f", round(fisher[fisher$gene == "HOXB13_carrier", "estimate"], 2))`, 95% LCB = `r sprintf("%.2f", round(fisher[fisher$gene == "HOXB13_carrier", "conf.low"], 2))`, adj. p = `{r} pvalr(fisher[fisher$gene == "HOXB13_carrier", "p.adjust"], digits = 2)`); the subsequent models focus on this gene. HOXB13 mutations occurred in `r round(wgs_summary$HOXB13_carrier_1 / wgs_summary$wgs_1 * 100, 1)`\% of participants.

The rare-variant effect was not independent of the polygenic score. In separate Cox models, a one-SD increase in PHS predicted a `{r} (round(wgs_results[1, "estimate"], 2) * 100) - 100`\% higher risk of PCa (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[1, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[1, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[1, "conf.high"], 2))`], p `{r} pvalr(wgs_results[[1, "p.value"]])`), while HOXB13 carriers had a `{r} round(wgs_results[2, "estimate"], 1)`-fold greater risk than non-carriers (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[2, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[2, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[2, "conf.high"], 2))`], p `{r} pvalr(wgs_results[[2, "p.value"]])`). When both predictors were included, only PHS remained significant (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[3, "estimate"], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[3, "conf.low"], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[3, "conf.high"], 2))`], p `{r} pvalr(wgs_results[[3, "p.value"]])`) whereas the HOXB13 effect was attenuated (HR = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_results[4, "estimate"], 2))`, p = `{r} pvalr(wgs_results[[4, "p.value"]])`). The interaction term was not significant. Individuals in the top 1.7\% of PHS values had an `{r} round(wgs_phs_95[[1, "value"]], 1)`-fold higher risk than those at the median (HR~98.3/50~ = `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs_95[[1, "value"]], 2))`, 95% CI [`{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs_95[[1, "conf.low"]], 2))`, `{r} sprintf("%.2f", round(wgs_phs_95[[1, "conf.high"]], 2))`]), exceeding the risk conferred by HOXB13 mutations. 

## Predicting population risk of prostate cancer onset based on HR from the HUSK cohort

We estimated risk stratification for PCa in the general population using HRs from our PHS models. For the population baseline incidence, we used exponential models fit to data from Huynh-Le et al. (2020). We then stratified these incidence curves by the HRs corresponding to the top 20% and bottom 20% of PHS from the Cox proportional hazards model fit to the HUSK data (@{tbl-1}). Analyses were conducted separately for any-stage PCa and aggressive PCa (@{fig-strat}).

Panel A of @{fig-strat} shows cumulative incidence of any-stage PCa by age and PHS stratum. For example, at age 75, an individual in the top 20% of PHS has an estimated cumulative risk of approximately 30%, compared with about 8% for someone in the bottom 20%. Relative to the population baseline, individuals in the top PHS quintile show substantially higher predicted incidence---roughly double the cumulative incidence by age 75. It is important to note that the apparent decline in incidence rate after age 70 in panel A is likely an artifact of reduced screening rather than a true decrease in disease occurrence (Huynh-Le et al., 2020).

# Discussion

We observed strong stratification in both Norwegian cohorts, which demonstrates the potential of PHS601 in a precision screening paradigm in Norway. The strong stratification in the HUSK cohort demonstrates good risk stratification in the general population. In addition, the NFCS cohort was recruited based on self-reported family history of cancer and showed elevated cancer risk relative to the general Norwegian population (@{suppfig-comp}). Therefore, even in a group with a family history of cancer, there is good stratification between low and high risk.

For aggressive disease, we also found good stratification between high- and low-risk individuals based on PHS, and we see a similar magnitude effect in both NFCS and HUSK cohorts. This suggests PHS601 could be effective at identifying individuals at greater risk of aggressive disease and therefore with the greatest clinical benefit for further screening via PSA or imaging. Although PHS601 is not specific for aggressive disease, it does appear to stratify for absolute risk of aggressive or metastatic prostate cancer [@dornisch2025; @seibert2018; @seibert2023; @pagadala2023].

In addition to testing the performance of PHS, we also compared PHS to screening for RPVs such as HOXB13. Even in the case of low sample sizes---for example, in the NFCS cohort we had only `{r} p212_sample_size[1, 3]` cases of prostatic cancer and `{r} p212_sample_size[2, 3]` cases of aggressive disease---the polygenic score was more informative than RPVs. A much larger percentage of the population are affected by a high risk score than are affected by currently known RPVs---high polygenic risk affects 50x more people than BRCA2 mutations [@seibert2023]---which means genetic risk scoring may be more useful at the population level. Therefore, PHS has potentially larger public health benefit.

Even though the combined model of PHS and HOXB13 was not significant, clinical interventions may differ between individuals whose phenotype arises from rare deleterious mutations versus those whose phenotype arises from the interaction of environment with the normal array of segregating genes of minor effect. For example, individuals with BRCA mutations may benefit from PARP inhibitors [@turk2018]. Furthermore, RPVs and PHSes have different implications for genetic counseling, particularly regarding the risk to offspring in the case of RPVs. Therefore, there remains value in screening for these rare variants in appropriate clinical contexts.

We observed a time-dependency for PHS in the any-stage PCa model, though not for aggressive disease. While the time-varying effect of PHS was weak, we observed a significant negative trend in the HR of PHS with age in two independent cohorts such that the strongest effect of genetic risk was at the youngest ages (@suppfig-zph). This age-dependent attenuation of genetic risk is consistent with observations from other complex diseases and may reflect several biological processes. First, as individuals age, the cumulative burden of environmental exposures, somatic mutations, and stochastic cellular processes may increasingly dominate over germline genetic variation in determining disease risk [@jiang2021; @winkler2024]. Second, competing risks of death from other causes may differentially affect high-risk (i.e., high-PHS) individuals, leading to a selected survivor population at older ages. Stronger genetic effects at younger ages have been well-documented for BRCA1/2 mutations in breast cancer [@kuchenbaecker2017] and across multiple complex diseases [@jiang2021]. Although we observed reduced incidence rates of any-stage PCa after age 70, likely due to decreased screening in this age group [@huynh-le2020a], for this to be an explanation of the time-dependency, there would need to be systematic differences in screening by genetic risk status within the older age group. The non-significant trend for aggressive disease may be explained by more complete case ascertainment for clinically-significant disease, as individuals with aggressive PCa are more likely to be captured in registry data [@huynh-le2020a], reducing age-related detection bias. Alternatively, this could reflect low power due to the small number of aggressive disease cases. These findings have important clinical implications for prostate cancer, as they identify the age range where genetic risk stratification may be most actionable for prevention and early detection.

## Future Directions

While PHS captures inherited genetic risk, prostate cancer risk is also influenced by social determinants of health, lifestyle factors, and environmental exposures [@plym2023; @pagadala2024; @pagadala2024a]. Future work should investigate how these modifiable factors interact with genetic risk to refine risk prediction models and identify opportunities for risk reduction, particularly in younger individuals with high genetic risk who stand to benefit most from early intervention.

The strong risk stratification observed in these population-based cohorts provides a foundation for prospective trials of risk-stratified screening in Norway. Such trials are essential to demonstrate clinical utility and to inform implementation strategies for precision screening programs.

Before implementing population-wide genetic screening, rigorous cost-effectiveness analyses are needed to assess the economic value of PHS-based screening in the Norwegian healthcare context. While existing analyses have estimated costs around $100,000 USD per quality-adjusted life year (QALY) for prospective genetic screening in breast cancer, ovarian cancer, and Lynch syndrome [@guzauskas2022; @galvisrojas2025], these estimates vary by healthcare system and screening strategy. Collaboration with health economists could refine these estimates for Norway and identify optimal screening thresholds and age ranges that maximize clinical benefit while maintaining cost-effectiveness.

While PHS601 performed well in Norwegian cohorts, future work could leverage federated learning approaches across multiple Norwegian biobanks to develop larger training datasets and potentially identify Nordic-specific genetic variants. The infrastructure developed in this study (code available on GitHub) provides a foundation for such collaborative efforts across secure data platforms.

One limitation of this study is that we did not have access to family history data or prostate-specific antigen measurements for all participants. While previous studies suggest family history adds limited information beyond PHS601 [@vassy2024], future work should explore optimal integration strategies for PHS with other clinical risk factors. The Norwegian Cancer Registry's comprehensive population-level cancer tracking provides an excellent foundation for such studies and for monitoring outcomes in precision screening programs.

# Conclusions

We demonstrate that PHS601 performs well in independent, population-based cohorts from Norway, providing strong risk stratification not only for prostate cancer but also for absolute risk of aggressive disease. These findings support the development of prospective trials of risk-stratified screening in Norway. Given that high polygenic risk affects 50x more individiuals than known rare pathogenic variants, PHS-based screening has the potential for substantial population health impact. We recommend that future work focus on: (1) prospective clinical trials to demonstrate real-world effectiveness, (2) health economic evaluations to guide implementation, and (3) integration of genetic risk with modifiable lifestyle factors to maximize opportunities for risk reduction in high-risk individuals.

::: {#suppfig-zph}

![](manuscript/figures_and_tables/zph_tt.pdf){width=85%}

Assessment of the proportional hazards assumption for PHS using Schoenfeld residuals plotted against age. The solid blue line represents the estimated time-varying log hazard ratio from the extended Cox model with a linear time transform (95% confidence bands shown). The dashed blue line shows the log hazard ratio from the standard Cox proportional hazards model, and the dashed red line indicates a hazard ratio of 1.0 (log HR = 0). Divergence between the solid and dashed blue lines indicates violation of the proportional hazards assumption and time-dependency of the PHS effect. Panels **(A)** and **(B)** show results for any-stage PCa in the HUSK and NFCS cohorts, respectively; panels **(C)** and **(D)** show results for aggressive PCa in the same cohorts. 

:::
